name: Checking Claims Against the Ledger
title: Checking Claims Against the Ledger
answer: Checking claims against the ledger means comparing a sustainability or carbon claim with the accounting records that support it. The claim might be a public statement about emissions, a disclosure in an annual report, a carbon credit retirement, or an internal target. The work covers the boundary of the claim, the period it covers, the units used, and the evidence that ties it to invoices, meter readings, purchase orders, or registry entries. It sits inside sustainability and carbon accounting, where the ledger is not only the general ledger but also the carbon ledger and the supporting documents behind it.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Checking claims against the ledger means comparing a sustainability or carbon claim with the accounting records that support it. The claim might be a public statement about emissions, a disclosure in an annual report, a carbon credit retirement, or an internal target. The work covers the boundary of the claim, the period it covers, the units used, and the evidence that ties it to invoices, meter readings, purchase orders, or registry entries. It sits inside sustainability and carbon accounting, where the ledger is not only the general ledger but also the carbon ledger and the supporting documents behind it.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a mix of financial systems and sustainability data sources. General ledger and ERP exports provide spend and quantity data, while utility portals, fuel cards, travel systems, supplier invoices, and carbon registries provide activity data. Emissions factor libraries and unit conversion tables sit alongside these sources, often in spreadsheets or a sustainability platform. The site's catalogue of 732 AI tools is one place to see what is available, though many teams still begin with a controlled spreadsheet and a document store.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical check starts by writing the claim in plain terms and fixing its boundary, period, and unit. The reviewer then maps each part of the claim to ledger accounts, activity data, and emission factors, and traces a sample back to source documents. AI can help extract text from invoices, match records, and flag outliers, but a person reviews the exceptions and the judgment calls. The output is a reconciliation that shows what supports the claim, what does not, and what remains uncertain.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk turn on provenance, access, and audit trail. The team needs the right to use supplier data, the right to rely on registry records, and a clear record of who changed what and when. Inaccurate claims can lead to greenwashing allegations, restatements, or regulatory attention, and the site's 219 compliance and regulation pages show how many rule sets can touch a single claim. Provenance also covers the AI tools used, including their training data, model version, and the human review applied to their output.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward continuous checking rather than annual sampling. Carbon ledgers, digital tags, and application programming interfaces are making it easier to link a claim to a transaction at the moment it is recorded. AI agents may draft reconciliations and monitor for drift, while assurance providers look for evidence that the process is controlled and repeatable. The open question is how quickly standards, registries, and audit practice converge on a common way to prove a claim against the ledger.
